items.passage:
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

[Drama excerpt: The interview]
[An office. Two INTERVIEWERS sit on one side of a table. SIPHO, 21, sits on the other. He is in a borrowed jacket.]

INTERVIEWER A: Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone in authority.

SIPHO: My rugby coach.

INTERVIEWER A: Go on.

SIPHO: He wanted me at lock. I wanted to play at flanker. I told him so. He listened. He said no.

INTERVIEWER B: And what happened?

SIPHO: I played lock.

INTERVIEWER B: How did that feel?

SIPHO: At the time? Not great.

INTERVIEWER B: And now?

SIPHO: [pauses] He was right. I would have been worse at flanker. I didn't see it then.

INTERVIEWER A: [writes something. Underlines it.] Most people in your position would have said they convinced the coach.

SIPHO: Most people in my position wouldn't be in this interview.

[Brief silence. INTERVIEWER B smiles. INTERVIEWER A does not, but his hand has stopped moving.]

INTERVIEWER A: Why this company, Mr Dlamini?

SIPHO: Because the person you put in the room said I would have to convince you I was honest. She didn't say I would have to convince you I was the cleverest applicant.

INTERVIEWER B: And which are you?

SIPHO: Honest. The other thing, I can learn.

[Drama excerpt: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

items.passage:
[Drama excerpt: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

[Drama excerpt: After class]
[A Grade 11 classroom, end of school day. MR OKAFOR, the substitute teacher, is wiping the board. OLUSEGUN, 17, stands by the door.]

OLUSEGUN: Sir.

MR OKAFOR: [without turning] Olusegun.

OLUSEGUN: I wanted to ask you something.

MR OKAFOR: Come in. Close the door if you want, or leave it open. It's the same to me.

[OLUSEGUN closes the door. He stays near it.]

OLUSEGUN: Why didn't you give me a detention? On the first day. The paper. You know.

MR OKAFOR: [still wiping] I remember.

OLUSEGUN: Mrs Hendricks would have.

MR OKAFOR: Mrs Hendricks knows you. She knows what works on you. I didn't, and I don't, much.

OLUSEGUN: So you just — looked at me.

MR OKAFOR: It's what I had.

OLUSEGUN: It was worse than a detention.

MR OKAFOR: [puts down the cloth] I'm sorry.

OLUSEGUN: I didn't say it was bad.

[Pause. MR OKAFOR turns to face him. He does not say anything. OLUSEGUN looks at the floor.]

OLUSEGUN: I think I want to apologise. Properly. For the paper. For — the whole first week.

MR OKAFOR: I'm not the one you need to apologise to.

OLUSEGUN: Tswelopele.

MR OKAFOR: Tswelopele.

OLUSEGUN: She doesn't talk to me.

MR OKAFOR: That, also, is fair.

[Long pause. OLUSEGUN nods, slowly. He turns and leaves. MR OKAFOR watches him go, then turns back to the board.]

[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. [Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. He went home that first evening tired in a way he had never been tired before, and lay on the bed without taking off his shoes, and thought, before he fell asleep, that he had become a different person between morning and evening, and that he did not yet know whether to be sorry about it.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. He went home that first evening tired in a way he had never been tired before, and lay on the bed without taking off his shoes, and thought, before he fell asleep, that he had become a different person between morning and evening, and that he did not yet know whether to be sorry about it.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. He went home that first evening tired in a way he had never been tired before, and lay on the bed without taking off his shoes, and thought, before he fell asleep, that he had become a different person between morning and evening, and that he did not yet know whether to be sorry about it.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. He went home that first evening tired in a way he had never been tired before, and lay on the bed without taking off his shoes, and thought, before he fell asleep, that he had become a different person between morning and evening, and that he did not yet know whether to be sorry about it.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The river]
When the river finally rose, it did so without ceremony. There was no rush of water down from the hills, no sudden thunder of wave-front; the river simply began, one Tuesday morning, to be wider than it had been the day before, and then wider again on Wednesday, and by Thursday the path Naledi had walked every day of her life — past the willow with the white stones at its base, across the small wooden bridge her grandfather had repaired the year he came home from the war — was gone. She stood at the place where the bridge had been and watched the brown water move past, smooth and unhurried, as if it had always been moving this way, as if the bridge had never been there at all. Her mother had wept when the bridge was carried off. Her father had stood at the window and said nothing. Naledi understood, now, that the river had not destroyed the bridge. It had simply continued, and the bridge had failed to continue alongside it. That, she suspected, was what disasters were. Not events. The absence of events that everyone had relied upon.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The factory]
The first day Mzwakhe stood inside the factory, what struck him was not the noise but the order. There was a precise place for everything. The hooks above the door for the safety equipment; the painted lines on the floor for the trolleys; the numbered stations along the line where each worker stood, hour after hour, repeating the small set of movements he had been trained to repeat. The order had been designed, he could see, to require nothing of him beyond his hands. He could think of his children while he worked. He could think of his mother's garden, or of the radio programme he had heard the night before, or of nothing at all. The line did not care. The line wanted only the rhythm. He understood, watching the foreman watch the stations from the high office at the end of the floor, that the order was not for him. It was for the foreman. It was for the people above the foreman, whom he would never meet. He went home that first evening tired in a way he had never been tired before, and lay on the bed without taking off his shoes, and thought, before he fell asleep, that he had become a different person between morning and evening, and that he did not yet know whether to be sorry about it.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: Market day]
Beatrice had been selling fish at the same stall on the Saturday market for nineteen years. She knew her customers as her grandmother had known her customers — not by name, though she remembered most of the names, but by what they bought, and how often, and what they were prepared to spend, and what they would say to a price that was higher than they had hoped for. She knew which of them had been doing well that month, and which had not, and she adjusted her dealings accordingly without ever announcing that she was doing so. The fishmongers further down the row sometimes laughed at her for what they called her softness. She did not argue with them. She knew, in a way they had not yet learned, that a market was not a place where money passed between strangers. A market was a place where a town spoke to itself about who was carrying whom, and who could afford to wait, and who could not. The money was the language. The people were the conversation. Beatrice had decided long ago that she would rather be remembered for what she had given than for what she had collected, and the books, in the end, had balanced anyway.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The waiting room]
The clinic waiting room had not been painted in fifteen years, and the chairs along the wall were the same chairs that had been there when Khanyi was a child and her mother had brought her for her first vaccination. She remembered the chairs because they had hurt the back of her knees, and they still hurt the back of her knees, now that she was here on her own behalf and not her mother's. The fan above the counter turned slowly. A child two seats down was reading a book aloud to his grandmother in a whisper neither of them seemed to find unusual. Khanyi closed her eyes and listened to him. It was a story about a boy who found a key that fitted no door he knew, and who spent his evenings going from house to house in his village, trying the key against every door he could find. He did not find the door. He found, instead, that everyone in the village had a story about a key they had once found and had never used. Khanyi opened her eyes. The grandmother was looking at the boy with such tenderness that Khanyi had to look away. She did not know whether the story was a real story, from a book, or one the boy was inventing as he went. It did not, she decided, matter. The story was a true story either way.

items.passage:
[Novel excerpt: The lighthouse]
Her grandfather had walked to the lighthouse every Sunday for as long as Mara could remember, and for nineteen years she had assumed he had a reason. The lamp had been automated for decades. The keepers' cottage stood empty. The wooden door at the base of the tower was locked, and her grandfather did not have a key. When she had asked him, once, what he did up there, he had smiled in the patient way he had and said only: some things you do because they ought to be done. She had not, at fourteen, understood this answer. She had assumed it was a kind of evasion, the way old men sometimes hid their reasons even from themselves. She understood it differently now. Standing at the kitchen window on the morning of his eighty-third birthday, watching him pause halfway up the path with his hands on his hips, watching him gather himself and continue, slower than before but with the same steady tread, she understood that the answer had not been an evasion at all. He had been telling her the whole thing. Some things you did because they ought to be done. The fact that no one was watching, the fact that the lamp no longer needed you, the fact that the door at the top was locked — none of these reduced the obligation, because the obligation had never been to the lamp. It had been to the act of going.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

items.passage:
[Poem: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

items.passage:
[Poem: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
[Poem: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

items.passage:
[Poem: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

items.passage:
[Poem: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

items.passage:
[Poem: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

items.passage:
[Poem: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.
