=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

items.passage:
=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Inheritance]
He left me the bees.
Not the house, which was always going
to be divided four ways, and not the field,
which my brothers had wanted longer than I had.
He left me the hives at the back of the plot,
and the smoker, and the veil that fits my face,
and the small, slow, complicated knowledge
of how to walk among bees without disturbing them.

He had taught me, when I was eight,
to listen for the change in the sound
of a queenless hive. He had taught me,
when I was older, that the bees did not need
to be loved; they needed to be observed.
I think now that this is what he was teaching me.
Not beekeeping. Attention.

My brothers will have the house.
I have the way he stood beside the hives at dusk
with his hands in his pockets,
saying nothing,
listening for the sound
of a colony that knew where it was.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: First language]
There are words I learned before I learned to speak —
the click of the gate at five in the morning,
the kettle's complaint on the cold stove,
my grandmother's small song to the chickens,
which was not in any language
anyone else in the house could hear.

Later I learned the words other people use —
the school-words, the form-words, the words
you say at counters and clinics.
I learned them well. People praised me.
I won prizes for them.

But there are nights, still, when I dream
in the old words, and wake unable
to translate them. They were not given to me
to be translated. They were given to me
to be carried, and to be returned, one day,
to the gate, to the stove, to the chickens
who will not, by then, remember me at all.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Drought]
The first year we spoke of it.
The second year, less.
By the third we had grown
into people who did not name
what we did not have.

My father walked the fence each morning
as if walking it could call the rain.
My mother counted the sacks of seed
as if counting them could fill them.
I learned to listen for what was missing —
the dripping eaves, the slow weight
of cloud against the window,
the green sound of a wet field at dawn.

When the cloud came in from the north
on the last day of October,
low and dark and heavy,
we stood at the kitchen window
and did not speak.
Hope, we had learned,
was a word you said aloud
only after the thing arrived.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: Before the interview]
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask first.
I have practised the answer to the question
they will ask third.
I have not practised the question between,
which I will not see coming, and which is the one
the panel will remember.

On the bus I rehearse the room
before I have entered it.
I sit in the wrong chair. I shake the wrong hand first.
I say the thing I have decided not to say.
Then I undo all of it and begin again,
the way you might rebuild a small machine
in the dark.

I do not know yet whether they will offer me the job.
I know only that I have already become, on this bus,
the person who will accept it,
and the person who will not,
and both of those people are looking forward
to becoming, by tomorrow, only one.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: The late visitor]
She arrived in the kitchen with no warning,
as if she had always been on her way —
boots wet, hair flat with rain, a small bag
set down beside the chair as if it weighed nothing.

I had not seen her since the funeral.
She did not say so. She did not say much
of anything, except to ask for tea
and to comment on the new colour of the walls.

We sat. The kettle did the work of speaking.
Outside, the dark came down across the field.
She had not, I realised, told me she was coming
because she had not, herself, known until
the bus was halfway here. She apologised
for nothing. I asked for nothing. The tea cooled
between us, and we drank it anyway.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: The fence line]
We had not spoken in fourteen years.
The argument about the tractor
had become the argument about his wife,
and the argument about his wife
had become a silence
neither of us was prepared to break.

When the post nearest the river finally rotted through,
we both arrived on Saturday morning,
carrying the same tools,
without having agreed who would come.
We did not look at each other.
We worked.
The new post was set by noon.
The wire was tightened.
The soil was packed.

He produced a flask of coffee.
He offered me a cup.
I took it.
We drank standing on opposite sides
of the new post,
looking down the line of the old fence,
and neither of us said anything at all.

It was, I have come to understand,
the closest either of us ever came
to an apology.

=== Text 1 ===
[Poem A: Night walk]
After supper my father would walk
the length of the road and back,
in any weather, without explanation.
We learned not to ask. We learned
to leave the door unlocked.

I understand now, though he never said,
that what he was walking was the day —
letting it settle into the dust of the road,
letting it lift, slightly, off his shoulders,
letting it become, by the time he reached the gate again,
something a man could put down
before lying down beside his wife.

He never asked us to come with him.
We did not offer. Some things
you do alone. Some things
you do, eventually, with the road itself,
which has the patience to be your companion
without ever pretending to be your friend.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem B: City morning]
Before the first taxi sounds its horn,
before the gates are unlocked,
before the woman who sells bread
has rolled the metal up from her shop window —

there is a moment when the city belongs
to the cleaners and the dogs.
They move along the empty pavements
as if they had been left in charge,
and in a way, briefly, they have.

By six the first lights are on
behind the bakery windows.
By half past, the buses are leaning into traffic.
The cleaners are already gone,
and the dogs have taken their old places
under the shop awnings,
watching the day come in
with the patient, unimpressed expression
of those who have seen it all before.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama excerpt: Two sisters]
[NTOMBI's kitchen. Late evening. NTOMBI, 38, is at the sink. Her sister LERATO, 41, sits at the table with an unopened envelope in front of her.]

NTOMBI: You haven't opened it.

LERATO: I'll open it.

NTOMBI: It's been an hour.

LERATO: I'll open it when I'm ready.

[Pause. NTOMBI dries her hands.]

NTOMBI: Ma would have already known what was in it.

LERATO: Ma would have already decided what was in it, which isn't the same.

NTOMBI: It is, with her.

LERATO: [picking up the envelope] You think it's going to be bad.

NTOMBI: I don't know what it's going to be.

LERATO: You know what you want it to be.

NTOMBI: That's not the same as knowing what it is.

[LERATO turns the envelope over in her hands. She does not open it. NTOMBI watches her, then turns back to the sink and continues with the dishes.]

LERATO: If it's the result we wanted, you'll be glad.

NTOMBI: I'll be glad.

LERATO: And if it's the other one, you'll still be glad. Just not for the same reason.

NTOMBI: [without turning] That isn't fair.

LERATO: I didn't say it wasn't true.

[NTOMBI does not respond. The sound of running water continues. LERATO opens the envelope.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The interview offer (a sister waits)]
Lerato had not opened the envelope. It had been an hour now, and it lay on the kitchen table between the salt and the bread, exactly where Ntombi had placed it when the post had come. Lerato was aware, as she sat with her hands flat on the wood, that her sister was aware of her not opening it. The dishes were being done with a precision that was not quite ordinary. Lerato knew what Ntombi was thinking, though Ntombi had not said. Ntombi was thinking that whatever was in the envelope, she — Ntombi — would respond to the news in a way that would have less to do with Lerato's news than with Ntombi's own life, the life that had not, in the end, gone in the direction Ntombi had once expected it would. Lerato knew this not because Ntombi was unkind but because Ntombi was honest, even with herself, even now. Lerato turned the envelope over. She did not open it. The dishes continued.

=== Text 1 ===
[Drama A: Father and son]
[Kitchen. Evening. BABA, 64, is at the table with a newspaper. His son MUSA, 28, stands in the doorway with his coat still on.]

MUSA: I'm taking the job.

BABA: [does not look up] Mm.

MUSA: I said I'm taking it.

BABA: I heard you.

[MUSA waits. BABA turns a page.]

MUSA: Aren't you going to say something?

BABA: What would you like me to say?

MUSA: Something. Anything. That you're glad. That you're not glad. That you think I'm making a mistake.

BABA: [putting the paper down] Are you making a mistake?

MUSA: No.

BABA: Then I have nothing to say about it.

MUSA: That's not fair.

BABA: I don't see why.

MUSA: Because Ma is in the next room not saying anything, and you are in here not saying anything, and somehow this is supposed to be a conversation.

BABA: [carefully] Your mother will say something tomorrow.

MUSA: And you?

BABA: [picks up the paper again] I have said what I have to say.

[MUSA stands in the doorway a moment longer. He does not take off his coat. He leaves. BABA does not turn another page for a long time.]

=== Text 2 ===
[Drama B: The village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

STRAW_MAN_L13.studentMessage: You made the opposing view too weak. Make it as strong as possible first.
steps: 1. Imagine the BEST supporter of the opposing view.
2. Write the strongest version of their argument.
3. THEN rebut.
STRAW_MAN_L13.sentenceFrame: The strongest version of the opposing view is that ____________ . However, ____________ .

REBUTTAL_UNSUPPORTED_L13.studentMessage: Your rebuttal needs at least 2 reasons.
steps: 1. Use: 'This ignores …' / 'This overlooks …' .
2. Give Reason 1.
3. Give Reason 2.

EVIDENCE_ABSENT_REBUTTAL_L13.studentMessage: Add evidence that shows the opposing view fails.
steps: 1. Pick one: statistic, study, example, expert view, comparative case.
2. Place it in the rebuttal so it directly attacks the opposing view.

SELF_CONTRADICTING_FET.studentMessage: Your rebuttal seems to support the OTHER side. Check that it defends your own thesis.
steps: 1. Re-read your thesis.
2. Re-read your rebuttal.
3. Ask: does my rebuttal protect my thesis? If not, rewrite the rebuttal so it supports your own side.
SELF_CONTRADICTING_FET.sentenceFrame: (After re-reading) My thesis says ____________ . My rebuttal supports this because ____________ .

items.prompt:

Write ONE counter-argument paragraph defending your position against the strongest opposing view. Your paragraph must: (1) open with a concession signal (admittedly / it is true that / some argue that / a serious objection); (2) represent the opposing view in its STRONGEST form — no straw man, no extreme caricature; (3) introduce the rebuttal with a connector (however / nevertheless / yet); (4) support the rebuttal with at least 2 substantive reasons; (5) include at least 1 piece of evidence (statistic, study, example, expert view, comparative case). The counter-argument must not undermine your own thesis.

alternateValidPatterns.name: rebuttal-via-reframing

STRAW_MAN_L13.studentMessage: You made the opposing view too weak. Make it as strong as possible first.
steps: 1. Imagine the BEST supporter of the opposing view.

3. THEN rebut.

REBUTTAL_UNSUPPORTED_L13.studentMessage: Your rebuttal needs at least 2 reasons.
steps: 1. Use: 'This ignores …' / 'This overlooks …' .

EVIDENCE_ABSENT_REBUTTAL_L13.studentMessage: Add evidence that shows the opposing view fails.
steps: 1. Pick one: statistic, study, example, expert view, comparative case.

SELF_CONTRADICTING_FET.studentMessage: Your rebuttal seems to support the OTHER side. Check that it defends your own thesis.
steps: 1. Re-read your thesis.

SELF_CONTRADICTING_FET.sentenceFrame: (After re-reading) My thesis says ____________ . My rebuttal supports this because ____________ .

items.prompt:

Your paragraph must: (1) open with a concession signal (admittedly / it is true that / some argue that / a serious objection); (2) represent the opposing view in its STRONGEST form — no straw man, no extreme caricature; (3) introduce the rebuttal with a connector (however / nevertheless / yet); (4) support the rebuttal with at least 2 substantive reasons; (5) include at least 1 piece of evidence (statistic, study, example, expert view, comparative case). The counter-argument must not undermine your own thesis. At Hard difficulty, address the strongest counter-argument that an expert in the field would make — not the layperson's objection.

items.passage:
[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.
