[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

[Corporate statement on workplace change]
We at TerraCorp value our people above all else. That is why, after extensive consultation with senior leadership, we have made the difficult decision to restructure certain operational units to better position the organisation for future opportunities. As part of this transition, approximately 240 colleagues will be affected by role changes, including separations from the company. These are painful decisions and have not been taken lightly. We are confident that the new structure will enable us to serve our clients more effectively and to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. We thank our departing colleagues for their dedicated service and wish them every success in their future endeavours. Affected individuals will be supported through our outplacement partner and offered access to wellbeing resources. We remain committed to our values, to our remaining colleagues, and to building a stronger TerraCorp for the years ahead.

[Promotional brochure: A new community development]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

[Campaign leaflet: Vote Mthembu]
STAND UP FOR OUR COMMUNITY

Mthembu is one of us. Born here. Schooled here. Married here. He has not forgotten where he comes from. While others sit in offices far away from your daily struggles, Mthembu walks the streets you walk and shops where you shop. He knows what the queues at the clinic look like. He knows what the buses are like in the rain. He knows what it costs to feed a family of five in this economy. His opponent has been to our community exactly twice in five years — both times for photographs. His opponent lives in a suburb you have never been to and sends his children to a school whose fees you could not pay for in a year. The choice is simple. Vote for the person who lives where you live. Vote for the person who has been where you have been. Vote for one of us. Vote Mthembu.

items.passage:
[Op-ed: The case for our heritage curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Developer's brochure]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Drama excerpt from village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent analyst's note]
Developments of this type, marketed as 'progress' or 'community', have a mixed record across the region. In approximately half of comparable projects, the promised amenities materialised at scale; in the rest, key facilities were either delayed, scaled back, or replaced with cheaper alternatives once the marketing phase ended and the regulatory attention had moved elsewhere. The language of the marketing material itself is worth noting. References to 'progress', 'modern families', and 'people who value what really matters' do substantial ideological work: they frame an investment decision as a moral or aspirational one, and they implicitly position those who decline or oppose the development as backward, outside the modern, or insufficiently aspirational. The ideological framing is independent of whether the development is otherwise a sound investment.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Defending the existing curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's response]
I have taught Grade 11 literature for sixteen years and I do not recognise the description of curriculum reform I read in last Sunday's paper. The activists supposedly urging this reform are not, in my experience, commentators with agendas. They are the parents of the pupils I teach, who are asking, reasonably, why their children encounter so few texts that reflect the world their children inhabit. A curriculum is not a fixed inheritance handed down unchanged. It is a set of choices, made by some people on behalf of others. The question is not whether to make those choices but whether to make them with our eyes open.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent commentary on the debate]
The disagreement over curriculum reform tends to be framed as a contest between progress and tradition, but this framing obscures what is actually at stake. Every curriculum is a selection. The question is not whether we are passing on culture but whose culture, defined how, and by whom. Defenders of the existing canon often argue, in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is evidence of quality. Critics often argue, also in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is sometimes evidence only of long-standing inclusion. A reasoned reform discussion would treat both claims as questions to be tested against specific texts and specific outcomes, rather than as positions to be defended in the abstract.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Developer's brochure]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Drama excerpt from village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent analyst's note]
Developments of this type, marketed as 'progress' or 'community', have a mixed record across the region. In approximately half of comparable projects, the promised amenities materialised at scale; in the rest, key facilities were either delayed, scaled back, or replaced with cheaper alternatives once the marketing phase ended and the regulatory attention had moved elsewhere. The language of the marketing material itself is worth noting. References to 'progress', 'modern families', and 'people who value what really matters' do substantial ideological work: they frame an investment decision as a moral or aspirational one, and they implicitly position those who decline or oppose the development as backward, outside the modern, or insufficiently aspirational. The ideological framing is independent of whether the development is otherwise a sound investment.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Defending the existing curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's response]
I have taught Grade 11 literature for sixteen years and I do not recognise the description of curriculum reform I read in last Sunday's paper. The activists supposedly urging this reform are not, in my experience, commentators with agendas. They are the parents of the pupils I teach, who are asking, reasonably, why their children encounter so few texts that reflect the world their children inhabit. A curriculum is not a fixed inheritance handed down unchanged. It is a set of choices, made by some people on behalf of others. The question is not whether to make those choices but whether to make them with our eyes open.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent commentary on the debate]
The disagreement over curriculum reform tends to be framed as a contest between progress and tradition, but this framing obscures what is actually at stake. Every curriculum is a selection. The question is not whether we are passing on culture but whose culture, defined how, and by whom. Defenders of the existing canon often argue, in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is evidence of quality. Critics often argue, also in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is sometimes evidence only of long-standing inclusion. A reasoned reform discussion would treat both claims as questions to be tested against specific texts and specific outcomes, rather than as positions to be defended in the abstract.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Developer's brochure]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Drama excerpt from village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent analyst's note]
Developments of this type, marketed as 'progress' or 'community', have a mixed record across the region. In approximately half of comparable projects, the promised amenities materialised at scale; in the rest, key facilities were either delayed, scaled back, or replaced with cheaper alternatives once the marketing phase ended and the regulatory attention had moved elsewhere. The language of the marketing material itself is worth noting. References to 'progress', 'modern families', and 'people who value what really matters' do substantial ideological work: they frame an investment decision as a moral or aspirational one, and they implicitly position those who decline or oppose the development as backward, outside the modern, or insufficiently aspirational. The ideological framing is independent of whether the development is otherwise a sound investment.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Defending the existing curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's response]
I have taught Grade 11 literature for sixteen years and I do not recognise the description of curriculum reform I read in last Sunday's paper. The activists supposedly urging this reform are not, in my experience, commentators with agendas. They are the parents of the pupils I teach, who are asking, reasonably, why their children encounter so few texts that reflect the world their children inhabit. A curriculum is not a fixed inheritance handed down unchanged. It is a set of choices, made by some people on behalf of others. The question is not whether to make those choices but whether to make them with our eyes open.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent commentary on the debate]
The disagreement over curriculum reform tends to be framed as a contest between progress and tradition, but this framing obscures what is actually at stake. Every curriculum is a selection. The question is not whether we are passing on culture but whose culture, defined how, and by whom. Defenders of the existing canon often argue, in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is evidence of quality. Critics often argue, also in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is sometimes evidence only of long-standing inclusion. A reasoned reform discussion would treat both claims as questions to be tested against specific texts and specific outcomes, rather than as positions to be defended in the abstract.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Developer's brochure]
PROGRESS BEGINS HERE

Our exciting new community development brings together everything a modern family needs. From the moment you drive through the secure entrance, you will know you have arrived somewhere different — somewhere designed for people who value what really matters. Wide streets. Tree-lined avenues. A clubhouse for the whole family. Walking paths for the morning runner; quiet corners for the evening reader. The schools nearby are among the best in the region. The shopping centre, only minutes away, offers everything you need without the inconvenience of the city. The boundary fence is high, the cameras are modern, and the security personnel are on patrol twenty-four hours a day. We have thought of everything. All you need to do is move in. The land before our development was farmland — beautiful in its way, but no longer needed for the kind of life people want to live. Now it is something more. It is the beginning. It is PROGRESS. And it is waiting for you.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Drama excerpt from village meeting]
[A community hall. Folding chairs in rows. THANDIWE, 67, the chairperson, sits behind a small table. The hall is full. KOPANO, 34, stands at the back.]

THANDIWE: The proposal is on the table. We have heard the developers. We have heard the council. Now we hear ourselves. Kopano.

KOPANO: [coming forward] The developers say we will benefit.

THANDIWE: They have said so.

KOPANO: They have said so before. About the road. About the clinic. About the school sports field.

[Murmurs from the chairs.]

THANDIWE: Kopano —

KOPANO: I am not finished, MaThandiwe.

THANDIWE: Go on.

KOPANO: The clinic is two rooms. The road is gravel. The sports field is a maize field again because the goalposts rotted. We are being asked to believe a fourth time.

THANDIWE: And you are saying we should not.

KOPANO: I am saying we should ask for a different agreement. A signed one. With dates. With consequences.

[An OLDER MAN at the front stands up.]

OLDER MAN: And if they refuse the agreement?

KOPANO: Then we have learned what they were going to do anyway, without spending the next three years finding out.

[Long pause. THANDIWE looks at the OLDER MAN. The OLDER MAN sits down. THANDIWE turns back to the hall.]

THANDIWE: Those in favour of the motion that we require a signed agreement before further consultation, please raise your hands.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent analyst's note]
Developments of this type, marketed as 'progress' or 'community', have a mixed record across the region. In approximately half of comparable projects, the promised amenities materialised at scale; in the rest, key facilities were either delayed, scaled back, or replaced with cheaper alternatives once the marketing phase ended and the regulatory attention had moved elsewhere. The language of the marketing material itself is worth noting. References to 'progress', 'modern families', and 'people who value what really matters' do substantial ideological work: they frame an investment decision as a moral or aspirational one, and they implicitly position those who decline or oppose the development as backward, outside the modern, or insufficiently aspirational. The ideological framing is independent of whether the development is otherwise a sound investment.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Defending the existing curriculum]
It has become fashionable in certain academic circles to argue that our heritage curriculum is in need of modernisation. We are told that the works our children have read for generations are no longer relevant, that the values they teach are out of step with the times, that the canon itself must be reconsidered. The argument, though dressed in the language of progress, is dangerous and shallow. The works our children read are not incidental decoration. They are the means by which a society passes on its understanding of itself — its history, its struggles, its hard-won values. To abandon them in favour of whatever happens to be popular this season is to abandon, in a single generation, the cultural inheritance that millions of ordinary parents have spent their lives preserving. The activists who urge this abandonment are not, in the main, the parents whose children attend our schools. They are commentators with agendas of their own. The ordinary, sensible majority knows better. Our duty is to defend what works.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A teacher's response]
I have taught Grade 11 literature for sixteen years and I do not recognise the description of curriculum reform I read in last Sunday's paper. The activists supposedly urging this reform are not, in my experience, commentators with agendas. They are the parents of the pupils I teach, who are asking, reasonably, why their children encounter so few texts that reflect the world their children inhabit. A curriculum is not a fixed inheritance handed down unchanged. It is a set of choices, made by some people on behalf of others. The question is not whether to make those choices but whether to make them with our eyes open.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Independent commentary on the debate]
The disagreement over curriculum reform tends to be framed as a contest between progress and tradition, but this framing obscures what is actually at stake. Every curriculum is a selection. The question is not whether we are passing on culture but whose culture, defined how, and by whom. Defenders of the existing canon often argue, in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is evidence of quality. Critics often argue, also in good faith, that long-standing inclusion is sometimes evidence only of long-standing inclusion. A reasoned reform discussion would treat both claims as questions to be tested against specific texts and specific outcomes, rather than as positions to be defended in the abstract.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The logistical reply]
Few teachers I know would deny that teenagers need more sleep. The argument for later school starts is medically sound, and where it has been tried, the immediate effects on attendance and mood appear real. The problem is not the biology. The problem is that schools do not exist in biological isolation. === Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.
