=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The logistical reply]
Few teachers I know would deny that teenagers need more sleep. The argument for later school starts is medically sound, and where it has been tried, the immediate effects on attendance and mood appear real. The problem is not the biology. The problem is that schools do not exist in biological isolation. A high school that starts at 8:45 a.m. cannot share its bus fleet with a primary school that starts at 8:00 a.m. — and so either the primary school must move, or the buses must run duplicate routes, or the older pupils must walk. After-school sports, which currently end at five, would end at six; the pupils who travel home by public transport would arrive in the dark all winter. The argument is rarely whether the change is good for adolescents in isolation. The argument is whether the costs to everyone else — to younger siblings, to working parents, to coaches and bus drivers — are worth the gain. These are not arguments against the policy. They are reasons why the policy is so seldom adopted.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro-ban editorial]
When the school council voted last term to ban smartphones during the school day, the predictable response from pupils was outrage. We were told that phones are essential — for safety, for note-taking, for staying in touch with parents. Yet the case for the policy is stronger than the howls of protest suggest. Research from the London School of Economics, examining results before and after similar bans in English schools, found measurable gains in test scores, with the largest gains concentrated among lower-attaining pupils. The implication is striking: the pupils who most need attention in class are the ones whose phones do the most damage. Some argue that responsibility, not prohibition, is the answer. Pupils, they say, must learn to manage distraction. But this misunderstands the design of the devices in their pockets, which are engineered by some of the world's most sophisticated psychological research teams to capture and hold attention. Asking a fifteen-year-old to out-discipline a billion-dollar attention industry is not a fair fight. The phones can wait until the bell.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Parent's letter]
My daughter is fourteen years old and she walks to school alone. She takes two buses. The first leaves at quarter to seven; the second is sometimes late. Last winter she missed it altogether and stood at the stop for forty minutes in the dark. The only reason I could find her was that she had her phone. The new policy at her school says she must hand her phone in at the gate each morning. I understand the argument. I have read the research too. But the research has not stood in the dark with a fourteen-year-old daughter who is not where she is supposed to be. I do not object to the school controlling phone use in class. I object to the assumption that her phone is hers to surrender, when in fact it is mine, and the reason I gave it to her was so that I would know she was safe. There is room for a more sensible policy than the one we have. The school could collect phones at the start of each lesson and return them at the end. It could allow phones at break. Instead it has chosen the easiest blanket rule, and expected parents to nod along. I am writing to say that I do not.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: In favour]
In 2013 Tallinn became the first European capital to abolish public transport fares for its residents. A decade on, the policy is still the subject of intense debate. Supporters argue that free transport is a matter of fairness: those who can least afford a car are most likely to depend on the bus, and a flat fare hits them hardest. Critics reply that nothing is truly free; the cost is simply transferred to taxpayers, many of whom never use the service. Yet the deeper question is what we ask transport to do. If buses and trains exist only to move individuals from A to B, then user fees are reasonable. If they exist to reduce congestion, lower emissions, and stitch a city together, then treating them as a shared utility — like streetlights or parks — is far more defensible. The Tallinn experiment has not produced miracles, but neither has it collapsed. That alone should give policymakers elsewhere pause for thought.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: Against]
It sounds attractive — free buses, free trains, no fare boxes, no awkward queueing for tickets — until you ask who pays. The answer, unavoidably, is everyone. Free public transport is not free; it is funded from general taxation, which means that residents who never use the bus subsidise those who do. In a city where many of the wealthiest households drive everywhere and many of the poorest do not in fact ride the bus either — they walk, or share lifts, or do not move at all — the policy turns out to subsidise the middle. Worse, free transport discourages investment in service quality. Where there are no fares, there is no fare-derived signal of demand. Routes that are over-used remain so; routes that are under-used remain so. The buses in Tallinn, after a decade of free travel, are reportedly still slow, still crowded, and still beset by reliability problems. The promise of free travel was that the bus would become a first choice. The reality is that for many residents it remains a last resort, only now paid for by everyone.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The sceptical case]
Homework has been a fixture of schooling for so long that the question of whether it works is rarely asked. When it is asked, the answer turns out to be uncomfortably complicated. Reviews of the research consistently find that, for primary-aged children, the effect of homework on academic achievement is small at best and sometimes negative. For older pupils the picture changes: short, focused tasks do appear to support learning, particularly in mathematics. But the kind of homework that crowds out evenings — long, undifferentiated, marked by parental anxiety — has weaker evidence behind it than its prevalence would suggest. The defenders of homework argue that it teaches discipline, independence, and time management. These are reasonable claims, but they are not what homework is usually evaluated on. If homework is justified on character grounds rather than academic ones, schools should at least be honest about that.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: A teacher's defence]
I have taught Grade Seven mathematics for eleven years and I have watched the homework debate cycle round at least three times. Each cycle ends in the same place. Someone writes a column claiming that homework does not work, the claim is shared and debated for a month, parents and pupils enjoy a temporary holiday from it, and then the examination results return and homework returns with them. The reason is straightforward. Mathematics, like a language, is built through repeated practice. The twenty minutes of supervised work in class is rarely enough to consolidate a new procedure. The homework that follows is not punishment; it is the rehearsal. I will concede that much homework is badly designed. Too much of it is undifferentiated, too much of it is marked too slowly to be useful, and too much of it crowds the evening with tasks that the pupil cannot reasonably complete alone. These are problems of execution. They are not arguments against homework. They are arguments for doing it better.

=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: Pro later starts]
The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. The reasoning is rooted in adolescent biology: during puberty, the circadian rhythm shifts, and teenagers find it genuinely difficult to fall asleep before late evening. A school day that begins at 7:30 is not just inconvenient for them; it is out of alignment with the way their bodies have organised themselves. Districts that have shifted to later starts report improvements in attendance, mood, and academic engagement. Critics argue that later starts disrupt parents' work schedules, after-school sports, and bus routes. These objections are real, but they are logistical, not biological. The question is whether the convenience of adults should determine when the school day begins, or whether the needs of the pupils — for whom the institution exists — should.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The logistical reply]
Few teachers I know would deny that teenagers need more sleep. The argument for later school starts is medically sound, and where it has been tried, the immediate effects on attendance and mood appear real. The problem is not the biology. The problem is that schools do not exist in biological isolation. A high school that starts at 8:45 a.m. cannot share its bus fleet with a primary school that starts at 8:00 a.m. — and so either the primary school must move, or the buses must run duplicate routes, or the older pupils must walk. After-school sports, which currently end at five, would end at six; the pupils who travel home by public transport would arrive in the dark all winter. The argument is rarely whether the change is good for adolescents in isolation. The argument is whether the costs to everyone else — to younger siblings, to working parents, to coaches and bus drivers — are worth the gain. These are not arguments against the policy. They are reasons why the policy is so seldom adopted.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Text A: The case for reduction]
When the OECD reported that only about nine per cent of plastic waste produced globally is recycled, the figure was widely shared and quickly forgotten. The reasons for the low rate are well understood: much plastic is technically recyclable but not economically so, contaminated streams cost more to process than they return, and the petrochemical industry has every incentive to keep virgin plastic cheap. Recycling, in other words, is not really the answer; it is a salve. The genuine answer is to produce less plastic in the first place. Ireland's 2002 charge on plastic shopping bags showed that small price signals can produce dramatic shifts: within a year, plastic-bag use had fallen by around ninety per cent. The lesson is not specifically about bags, which are a minor fraction of total plastic waste. It is about what happens when the externalities of disposable convenience are made visible at the point of choice.

=== Source 2 ===
[Text B: The case for better recycling]
The argument that we cannot recycle our way out of the plastic problem is fashionable, and it is partly correct. Recycling alone will not solve a problem of the scale we face. But the leap from 'partly correct' to 'recycling is a salve' is a longer leap than the sceptics usually acknowledge. Better collection systems, deposit-return schemes, and mandatory recycled content in new products have all been shown to lift recycling rates substantially in jurisdictions that have implemented them seriously. The OECD's roughly nine per cent global recycling rate is not a verdict on what recycling can achieve. It is a verdict on how little most countries have tried. A world in which recycling is treated as a serious industrial enterprise — properly funded, properly regulated, and integrated into product design from the start — would look very different from the one we have. The conclusion that we should produce less plastic and the conclusion that we should recycle the plastic we do produce are not in competition. We need both.

items.prompt:
Speakers: a coach and a young athlete.
Topic: balancing sport with academic commitments

Write a dialogue (280–420 words) between the two named speakers on the topic above. Your dialogue must: (1) give each speaker a clear, distinct position; (2) provide at least 1 supporting reason per speaker; (3) contain at least 3 exchanges — neither speaker monologues; (4) include at least 2 moments where a speaker references the other's words explicitly ('You said X, but…'); (5) show development — at least one speaker qualifies, refines, or concedes part of their position by the end. At Hard difficulty, by the end of the dialogue, the two speakers should have located the specific point at which they disagree — and identified what would have to be true for them to agree.

Read the text. Identify at least 4 instances of vague, overused, or imprecise vocabulary (very / good / bad / nice / thing / stuff / get / do / kind of / a lot of). For each: (1) quote the imprecise word or phrase; (2) provide a precise replacement — the replacement must itself be specific, not another vague word; (3) state the semantic gain (more specific / more accurate / more concrete / more measured). At least 2 replacements should use AWL or discipline-specific terms.

Deliver an extended oral argument in text form (420–600 words, approximately 4–5 minutes). Your argument must: (1) state a clear position in the opening using a stance verb; (2) develop at least 3 supported arguments, each with reasoning or evidence; (3) acknowledge at least 1 counter-argument with concession + rebuttal; (4) use at least 2 rhetorical techniques (rhetorical question, direct address, tricolon, contrast, anaphora, climax); (5) close with a synthesising conclusion that adds depth rather than restating; (6) maintain formal-spoken register.

items.stimulus:
Topic: Should compulsory community service be introduced for school leavers?

Deliver an extended oral argument in text form (420–600 words, approximately 4–5 minutes). Your argument must: (1) state a clear position in the opening using a stance verb; (2) develop at least 3 supported arguments, each with reasoning or evidence; (3) acknowledge at least 1 counter-argument with concession + rebuttal; (4) use at least 2 rhetorical techniques (rhetorical question, direct address, tricolon, contrast, anaphora, climax); (5) close with a synthesising conclusion that adds depth rather than restating; (6) maintain formal-spoken register.
items.question:

Task: Write the 420–600 word extended oral argument with counter-argument, ≥2 techniques, synthesising conclusion.

answerKey.scoringPhilosophy: Each check scores independently and carries a component tag (reasoning / language / register / format). Diagnostic-only checks (AWL, hedging, formulaic patterns) influence confidence and surface learner suggestions but do NOT contribute to pass/fail. ESL/FAL learners receive band tolerance on language and register components; reasoning component is never penalised for surface grammar weakness.
answerKey.passFractionAppliesTo: Sum of non-diagnostic checks only. Diagnostic checks are excluded from the pass fraction calculation.

recoveryMapping.POSITION_ABSENT_ORAL_FET: State your view in one sentence. Use: I argue / I believe / In my view.
recoveryMapping.SUPPORT_LOW_ORAL_FET: Three-point frame: Point 1 / Point 2 / Point 3 (claim + reason for each).
recoveryMapping.COUNTERARG_ABSENT_ORAL_FET: Concession + rebuttal frame: 'It may be argued that X. However, Y because Z.'
recoveryMapping.SYNTHESIS_ABSENT_ORAL_FET: Your conclusion must go beyond restating your position — what does your argument reveal?

alternateValidPatterns.name: delayed-position
alternateValidPatterns.description: Position emerges within the first paragraph rather than the first sentence — valid where the opening frames the stakes first.

alternateValidPatterns.name: position-via-orientation
alternateValidPatterns.description: Position signalled by clear evaluative orientation (e.g. 'The case for X is stronger than its critics allow') without an explicit stance verb.

alternateValidPatterns.name: distributed-counter-argument
alternateValidPatterns.description: Counter-arguments addressed across multiple paragraphs rather than in one dedicated paragraph.

alternateValidPatterns.name: implied-counter-argument
alternateValidPatterns.description: Counter-argument acknowledged through anticipatory framing ('Critics who raise X tend to overlook Y') without a standalone counter paragraph.

alternateValidPatterns.name: rhetorical-via-restraint
alternateValidPatterns.description: Rhetorical effect built on restraint or understatement — counted as a technique when the absence is doing rhetorical work.

alternateValidPatterns.name: conclusion-via-implication
alternateValidPatterns.description: Conclusion that names an implication not stated in the body — adds depth without restating.

alternateValidPatterns.name: conclusion-via-question
alternateValidPatterns.description: Conclusion that re-poses the opening question in light of what the essay has shown.

alternateValidPatterns.name: non-linear-analytical-sequencing
alternateValidPatterns.description: Advanced learners may present claim → counter → evidence → re-claim, or evidence → pattern → claim. Valid when each component is present and connected, regardless of order.

alternateValidPatterns.name: subtle-literary-interpretation
alternateValidPatterns.description: Interpretations carried by sustained tone, image, or framing — rather than declarative statements — are valid when the textual basis is identifiable.

confidenceModifierHooks.action: Lower style-quality confidence at >0.45; do NOT fail.
Surface HEDGING_OVERUSE_FET above 15%; not a fail.
Surface AWL_BELOW_TARGET_SUPPORT_FET below target; ESL-exempt; not a fail.
Style note only; ESL-exempt; not a fail.
Surface THESIS_PARAPHRASE_FET above 0.45; lower confidence on universal-claim; not an auto-fail.
Bands GREEN <0.10 / AMBER 0.10–0.15 / RED >0.15. For ESL/FAL learners apply +3pt soft band tolerance. Never auto-fails reasoning checks.

POSITION_ABSENT_ORAL_FET.studentMessage: State your view in one short sentence at the start.
steps: 1. Use: I argue / I believe / In my view / I will defend the view that.
2. Place it in the opening.
1. Point 1: claim + because + reason.
2. Point 2: claim + because + reason.

COUNTERARG_ABSENT_ORAL_FET.studentMessage: Acknowledge an opposing view, then push back.
steps: 1. Start with: 'It may be argued that …' .
2. Continue with: 'However, …' .
3. Add a reason.
COUNTERARG_ABSENT_ORAL_FET.sentenceFrame: It may be argued that ____________ . However, ____________ because ____________ .

SYNTHESIS_ABSENT_ORAL_FET.studentMessage: Your conclusion repeats your opening. Add deeper insight.
steps: 1. Do not restate.
2. Add: 'What this shows is …' or 'Beyond this point, …'.

items.stimulus:
Scenario: You are applicant for a youth leadership scholarship. Four panel members ask you the following questions. Answer each in 50–80 words.

  Q1. Tell us about a time you led a project that did not go as planned. What did you learn?
  Q2. How do you respond when a senior person disagrees with your view?
  Q3. Describe one weakness you have actively worked to improve.
  Q4. If you receive this scholarship, what specifically will you do that you could not otherwise do?

Each answer must: (1) address the specific question — no generic platitudes; (2) maintain consistent tone across all 4 answers (same candidate); (3) include a specific example or piece of evidence (at least 3 of 4); (4) use formal interview register — no slang, no fillers; (5) demonstrate self-awareness in at least 1 answer.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-PHONES-PARENT]
Friends, fellow parents. We were told two years ago that the phone-free policy at our school would damage our children's social development, that it would alienate them from their peers, that it would create a generation unable to function in a connected world. Two years on, what we have observed is the opposite. The pupils are talking to each other at break. The library is fuller than it has been in a decade. The teachers report fewer disputes about who said what online. I am not here to claim the policy is perfect or that it has no costs. I am here to ask whether the costs we feared have in fact materialised, and to suggest that they have not. Before we vote on whether to relax the policy, I ask the council to consider what we would actually be giving up.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-PHONES-PARENT]
Friends, fellow parents. We were told two years ago that the phone-free policy at our school would damage our children's social development, that it would alienate them from their peers, that it would create a generation unable to function in a connected world. Two years on, what we have observed is the opposite. The pupils are talking to each other at break. The library is fuller than it has been in a decade. The teachers report fewer disputes about who said what online. I am not here to claim the policy is perfect or that it has no costs. I am here to ask whether the costs we feared have in fact materialised, and to suggest that they have not. Before we vote on whether to relax the policy, I ask the council to consider what we would actually be giving up.

[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-PHONES-PARENT]
Friends, fellow parents. We were told two years ago that the phone-free policy at our school would damage our children's social development, that it would alienate them from their peers, that it would create a generation unable to function in a connected world. Two years on, what we have observed is the opposite. The pupils are talking to each other at break. The library is fuller than it has been in a decade. The teachers report fewer disputes about who said what online. I am not here to claim the policy is perfect or that it has no costs. I am here to ask whether the costs we feared have in fact materialised, and to suggest that they have not. Before we vote on whether to relax the policy, I ask the council to consider what we would actually be giving up.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-PHONES-PARENT]
Friends, fellow parents. We were told two years ago that the phone-free policy at our school would damage our children's social development, that it would alienate them from their peers, that it would create a generation unable to function in a connected world. Two years on, what we have observed is the opposite. The pupils are talking to each other at break. The library is fuller than it has been in a decade. The teachers report fewer disputes about who said what online. I am not here to claim the policy is perfect or that it has no costs. I am here to ask whether the costs we feared have in fact materialised, and to suggest that they have not. Before we vote on whether to relax the policy, I ask the council to consider what we would actually be giving up.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-COUNCIL-DEVELOPMENT]
Members of the council. The community before you has lived with three failed promises in a decade. The clinic that is two rooms. The road that is gravel. The sports field that is a maize field again. We are not, this evening, asking you to trust us. We have given you no reason to distrust us either, but that is not the point. We are asking you to require, this time, a signed agreement, with dates, and with consequences for non-delivery. If the developers refuse such an agreement, you will have learned, in a single evening, what would otherwise have taken three years to discover. If they accept it, the agreement will hold them to what they have promised. Either outcome serves this community better than what we have had so far. The council has the standing to require this. The council has the obligation to require this. Thank you.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-CURRICULUM-DEBATE]
Honourable colleagues. The argument has been made that modernising our literature curriculum is dangerous, that it represents an abandonment of cultural inheritance, that the activists urging it are commentators with agendas. I want to address each of these claims directly. First: every curriculum is a selection. To say that the current one is tradition is to say only that it is the selection we have kept. It does not establish that it is the selection we should keep. Second: the parents in our schools — the ordinary, sensible majority the previous speaker invoked — are themselves asking the questions the previous speaker dismisses. The activists are the parents. Third: a literature curriculum is not a museum. It is an invitation to the next generation to recognise themselves, and the world they inhabit, in the texts they encounter. If our curriculum cannot do that, the failure is the curriculum's, not the generation's. I urge a reasoned, evidence-based review.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-PHONES-PARENT]
Friends, fellow parents. We were told two years ago that the phone-free policy at our school would damage our children's social development, that it would alienate them from their peers, that it would create a generation unable to function in a connected world. Two years on, what we have observed is the opposite. The pupils are talking to each other at break. The library is fuller than it has been in a decade. The teachers report fewer disputes about who said what online. I am not here to claim the policy is perfect or that it has no costs. I am here to ask whether the costs we feared have in fact materialised, and to suggest that they have not. Before we vote on whether to relax the policy, I ask the council to consider what we would actually be giving up.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-VOTING-AGE-DEBATE]
I am here to argue against lowering the voting age to sixteen, and I want to make clear at the start that I am doing so with respect for those who hold the opposite view. The argument I am most persuaded by is the habit-formation argument — that sixteen-year-olds, still embedded in the structures of school and family, are well placed to begin voting and to continue voting through adulthood. That argument has weight, and I will not dismiss it. My objection is different. It is that the disengagement we observe among voters in their early twenties is not a problem we should solve by extending the franchise downward. It is a problem that deserves to be addressed where it occurs. Lowering the age may produce a habit. It will not, by itself, produce the engagement the habit is meant to embody.

items.passage:
[Transcript: TC-LIBRARY-RESEARCH]
Reviews of community library closures in similar boroughs have found patterns rather than universal effects. Where alternatives are nearby and accessible, the consolidation of branches is broadly tolerated. Where alternatives are distant or poorly served by transport, library use does not transfer; it declines. This is not a controversial claim among researchers. It is the consistent finding. I do not say this to argue that Main Street must be kept open at any cost. I say it because the Council's framing of the closure as a consolidation is not, on the evidence, what closures of this kind have been. They have been withdrawals. If the Council wishes to defend the closure, it should defend it on those terms. The community deserves accurate language about what is being decided on their behalf.
